Based on the evidence provided, Judge Amit Mehta of the US District Court for the District of Columbia found Google's search business to be a monopoly because he ruled on 2024-08-05 that Google violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act by acting as a monopolist in general search services and general search text advertising [Source: ev-1]. The primary theory of harm was "default-distribution deals," where Google paid companies like Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla billions of dollars to remain their default search engine [Source: ev-1]. Specifically, trial evidence showed that Google paid approximately $26.3 billion for distribution in 2021 and gave Apple roughly 36% of Safari search-ad revenue [Source: ev-1]. Judge Mehta determined this conduct was exclusionary because it created a self-reinforcing loop where defaults generate scale, which creates data, improves quality, and ultimately protects the default status against rivals [Source: ev-1].

The remedies ordered by Judge Mehta on 2025-08-05 included requiring Google to sell Chrome (the first forced divestiture of a major tech company since the Microsoft case of 2000), prohibiting Google from paying for default search placement or entering into revenue-sharing agreements, and imposing limits on acquisitions and AI-related investments [Source: ev-1].
